findings.claim: The comment on this except-clause (lines 124-126) asserts a raise from `runner` is 'never charged to a task, because no task was ever started for it' — but `run_one_cell` (saffron/cell/session.py) creates `run_id`/`task_id` at lines 824-839, opens the phase loop's try block at line 855, and only its outermost `except BaseException: ... raise` (session.py:1765-1775) is what actually reaches this except-clause. That try block spans `plan_checkpoint` and every later phase, so a crash after one or more attempts have already opened and closed with real `cost_usd_est` (e.g. a runtime dying mid-REPAIR) still propagates as a raised exception. Because `run_batch` never learns that run's `run_id` on this path, `attach_run_to_batch` is never called, the run's `batch_id` stays NULL forever, and `ledger.batch_spend` (which sums attempts joined through `runs.batch_id`) permanently excludes real, already-spent money from the budget gate at line 108 — letting the batch admit further candidates against a budget that is actually already partly consumed. No test here catches this because `FakeRunner` raises a bare exception with no ledger rows behind it at all, unlike the real failure mode.

The breaker is only evaluated before starting the next candidate (line 113), while the counter itself is updated after each candidate returns (lines 136-143). If the two (or more) candidates that trigger the threshold are the last ones in `candidates`, the loop exits normally at line 145 and closes the batch as `DRAINED` instead of `INFRASTRUCTURE`, even though the standing abort count reached the threshold. This silently misreports why the night ended in the one column (`batches.status`) the design says exists precisely to distinguish 'the toolchain is broken' from an ordinary drain — no test exercises a queue whose trailing candidates are the ones that trip the breaker.

`until.isoformat()` writes `until_ts` in `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS` form (ISO with a 'T'), while every other timestamp this schema stores (`started_at`, `ended_at`, and every `datetime('now')` call elsewhere in ledger.py) is SQLite's `YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS` (space-separated). The schema's own comment on `batches` (ledger.py ~line 27-30) states timestamps are TEXT 'matching every other timestamp this module writes ... rather than inventing a second representation' — this line does exactly that. Nothing in this diff or the passing suite reads `until_ts` back for a string comparison against another timestamp column, so no gate or test can see it, but a future lexicographic comparison (e.g. `until_ts < datetime('now')` in a recovery or report query) will misorder because `'T' (0x54) > ' ' (0x20)` at the same character position for an otherwise-identical date-time.

This is the only test that verifies `attach_run_to_batch` is called with the right arguments, and it runs against a fresh ledger where this is the first batch ever created (batch_id=1) and the first run ever created (run_id=1). Because both ids are 1, swapping the call at saffron/batch.py:134 to `ledger.attach_run_to_batch(batch_id, outcome.run_id)` would still update `runs.batch_id` to 1 where `run_id = 1` — an identical result — so the test would keep passing while the argument order (and thus every real night, where run_id and batch_id differ) would be silently wrong. The test never exercises a case where run_id != batch_id, so it cannot actually confirm which id lands in which column.
